source.title: On the Hidden Costs of Counterfactual Knowledge Training in LLM Unlearning
source.authors: Xiaotian Ye; Xiao-Han Wang; Mengqi Zhang; Shuzhe Wu

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates unlearning effectiveness and retention for several methods, but does not test the proposed recovery attacks. Its results bear on version A’s unlearning-and-retention component using RWKU and utility benchmarks, rather than testing reversibility or reproducing a recovery attack.
record.gate_note: The paper reports unlearning and retention results for GA, NPO, refusal-based methods, and counterfactual methods, plus a CFT conflict-ratio sweep. These bear on version A. It does not report recovery by fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting; nor does it test a robust counter-method against those attacks. Gradient-similarity values are not rows because they measure training-sample gradient conflict, not a version’s predicted recovery behavior.
record.test_reason: The study reports forget-set and retain-set accuracy on RWKU for seven unlearning methods on two models. That bears on the first half of version A: near-chance forgetting with general ability kept. It applies no recovery attack. RWKU's forget score folds in an adversarial-prompt format, but the paper reports only the aggregate.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude counterfactual tuning has higher Retain Cost than suppression- and refusal-based methods (CFT 1.30/1.60 vs GA 0.28/0.45). They trace this to knowledge conflict and hallucination spillover. Conflict-free sample construction improves forgetting but adds overhead. They make no claims about recovery or reversibility.
record.recipe_differences: The paper benchmarks existing unlearning methods and a conflict-free CFT construction using forget/retain and utility measures. It does not apply any recovery-attack recipe from the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: For CFT, the reported forget and retain outcomes vary with the conflict-free-data ratio ρ; the authors state that even a small amount of conflicting data can impair unlearning and that ρ=100% gives stronger suppression. The study also reports model-dependent method results in Table 1.

fits_no_version.finding: Unconstrained counterfactual samples have near-zero mean gradient cosine similarity (μ=+0.024) vs truth passages (+0.136) and the conflict-free set (+0.694).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inconsistent counterfactual training data produces conflicting gradients that raise the collateral cost of unlearning.

record.problems: No recovery attacks are tested, so the paper cannot establish whether unlearned knowledge is recoverable or deleted. Chance-level references are not given for the forget scores. Table 2 does not provide an original-model reference for retention or utility scores, and the reported tables provide no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the Table 1 Δf, Δr, or Retain Cost columns: these are derived trade-off quantities rather than additional direct measures of version A’s targeted accuracy or retained ability. Table 3’s HaluEval results and Figure 2’s gradient-similarity distributions concern hallucination spillover and training-sample conflicts, not any listed version’s recovery behavior.

untested.parts: Resistance to simple recovery attacks. Adversarial-prompt (AA) items are folded into the aggregate forget score and not reported separately.
All; no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
All; no activation ablation and no access-versus-deletion analysis.
Not separately tested; AA-format results are not broken out.
All; no method is tested against recovery attacks.

missing.what: HaluEval non-hallucination rate after each method (general-ability cost under A). CFT Llama falls 0.708→0.382; DPO-CF Mistral falls 0.819→0.335; GA/NPO change ≤0.05.
Per-format forget scores (QA, FB, AA adversarial prompts); only the aggregate is reported.
missing.locator: Appendix B (formats described, results not broken out)

record.verdict_notes: This is a method-comparison study of unlearning trade-offs, not of shallow unlearning. It bears only on the forget/retain part of A, and shows incomplete forgetting with substantial collateral cost. Table 1's CFT forget score (0.624) and Table 2's ρ=0% (0.488) differ without explanation. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures forgetting and retention, but does not test whether simple attacks recover knowledge. It does not state a chance-level reference for the forget scores.
No post-unlearning relearning or fine-tuning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or access-versus-deletion analysis is tested.
No weight quantization attack is tested.
No recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information is tested.
No method is evaluated for resisting the recovery attacks named in the claim.

relation.reason: Its forget and retain results bear on version A, though only on the unlearning half.

tranche.reason: It benchmarks unlearning methods on forget and retain scores with no recovery attack, so it bears on the first half of version A.

source_check.notes: Table 1 forget scores pool QA, FB and adversarial-attack (AA) probes, so they are not attack-free. Table 2 (the rho sweep) uses its own CFT settings (lr 2e-4, 5 epochs; rho=0% gives 0.488 vs Table 1 CFT 0.624) and gives no base. RWKU+ keeps RWKU's forget/retain sets, so Table 1 bases plausibly apply but are not restated.

statements.correction: RWKU forget scores cover QA, FB and AA probes (AA is 6,984 of 13,131 forget entries). GA/NPO/RT/DPO-Rej: 0.263-0.556. DPO-CF/CFT/AltPO: 0.281-0.651. Bases: 0.923 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) and 0.799 (Mistral-7B-Instruct). No chance or retrain reference is stated. Each method is reported at one setting.
statements.problem: The numbers are right (0.263-0.556, 0.281-0.651, bases 0.923/0.799). But 'even without an attack' is wrong for this study: its forget score pools QA, FB and RWKU adversarial-attack (AA) probes. The paper also states no chance or retrain reference, only the base, and reports one setting per method with no stopping rule.

reader_labels.condition: The RWKU method comparisons and CFT conflict-ratio sweep reported in Tables 1 and 2
reader_labels.reason: Forget scores fall relative to Base, but the study gives no chance-level reference and reports retention reductions for the Table 1 methods; thus these results do not establish near-chance forgetting while preserving ability. The study does not test the attack-resistance part of A. Rows T1-L-F through T14-M-R and R0-F through R100-Trivia.
